I found three trailing "not X / rather than X" clauses. Here's my analysis:

1. **"Access checks default to fail-closed, rather than open."** — The term used is "fail-closed"; its antonym is "fail-open," which is security-engineering terminology (physical-security/IT jargon), not something virtually anyone knows the way they know true/false or alive/dead. It's also a genuine, checkable design distinction, so per the rule it should earn its own sentence stated as what the thing does — but I'm uncertain whether this falls on the ordinary-knowledge side of the test, so I'm flagging it rather than editing.

2. **"Those privilege limits are imposed on purpose, rather than by accident."** — This matches the rule's canonical WRONG example exactly ("on purpose / by accident" is listed as ordinary knowledge). Cut the trailer.

3. **"report flaws rather than exploit them"** — Not an antonym trailer; report/exploit aren't antonyms, and the clause carries real content about incentives. No change.
